# Overview



**scGPT** is a foundation model for single-cell multi-omics built with generative AI. It leverages a Transformer-based architecture to learn meaningful representations of single-cell gene expression data, enabling downstream tasks such as cell type annotation, multi-batch integration, perturbation prediction, gene regulatory network inference, and reference mapping — all from a single pretrained model. The project is published as a pip-installable Python package (v0.2.5) with pretrained checkpoints trained on up to 33 million cells.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L7), [scgpt/__init__.py](scgpt/__init__.py#L1-L30)

## What scGPT Does

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) produces high-dimensional expression matrices where each row is a cell and each column is a gene. scGPT reformulates this data into a **sequence modeling problem**: each cell becomes a "sentence" whose tokens are genes and whose token values are expression levels. A Transformer encoder then learns to reconstruct masked expression values — analogous to masked language modeling in NLP — producing rich cell-level and gene-level embeddings that transfer across tasks and tissues.

The core insight is that **genes in a cell interact in context-dependent ways**, and a self-attention mechanism can capture these interactions without hand-crafted feature engineering. After pretraining on tens of millions of cells, scGPT can be fine-tuned with minimal labeled data for task-specific applications.

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py](scgpt/model/model.py#L25-L95), [scgpt/model/model.py](scgpt/model/model.py#L290-L370)

## Architecture at a Glance

The diagram below traces the data flow from raw expression counts through tokenization, encoding, the Transformer backbone, and finally to task-specific decoder heads. Understanding this pipeline is the key to working with scGPT effectively.

> **Prerequisite**: This diagram uses Mermaid flowchart syntax. Each node represents a distinct module in the codebase; arrows indicate the primary data-flow direction during a forward pass.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input["Input Layer"]
        A["Raw AnnData<br/>(cells × genes)"] --> B["Preprocessor<br/>filter · normalize · log1p · bin"]
        B --> C["GeneVocab<br/>gene name → token id"]
        B --> D["ContinuousValueEncoder<br/>expression → embedding"]
    end

    subgraph Backbone["Transformer Backbone"]
        E["GeneEncoder<br/>token id → gene embedding"]
        F["Embedding Fusion<br/>gene_emb + value_emb<br/>or gene_emb × value_emb"]
        G["Domain-Specific BatchNorm<br/>(optional)"]
        H["Transformer Encoder<br/>PyTorch or Flash-Attention"]
        E --> F
        D --> F
        F --> G
        G --> H
    end

    subgraph Heads["Task-Specific Decoder Heads"]
        I["ExprDecoder<br/>reconstruct expression<br/>(MLM pretraining)"]
        J["ClsDecoder<br/>cell type classification"]
        K["MVCDecoder<br/>masked value prediction<br/>from cell embedding"]
        L["AdversarialDiscriminator<br/>batch correction (DAB)"]
        M["Cell Embedding<br/>cls · avg-pool · w-pool"]
        H --> I
        H --> J
        H --> K
        H --> L
        H --> M
    end

    C --> E
    A --> C

    style Input fill:#e8f4f8,stroke:#2196F3
    style Backbone fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
    style Heads fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py](scgpt/model/model.py#L25-L180), [scgpt/preprocess.py](scgpt/preprocess.py#L11-L100), [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py](scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py#L21-L85)

## Core Components

The table below maps each major subsystem to its source module, responsibility, and the key class or function you will interact with most often.

| Subsystem | Source Module | Key Class / Function | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Preprocessing** | `scgpt.preprocess` | `Preprocessor` | Filter, normalize, log1p, select HVGs, bin expression values |
| **Tokenization** | `scgpt.tokenizer` | `GeneVocab` | Map gene names ↔ integer token IDs; load/save vocab files |
| **Data Collation** | `scgpt.data_collator` | `DataCollator` | Pad, bin, and apply MLM masking per batch |
| **Model** | `scgpt.model` | `TransformerModel` | Full encoder–decoder with configurable heads |
| **Multi-omics Model** | `scgpt.model` | `MultiOmicTransformerModel` | Extended model with modality-specific encoders |
| **Generation Model** | `scgpt.model` | `TransformerGenerator` | Perturbation-aware model with perturbation token encoder |
| **Loss Functions** | `scgpt.loss` | `masked_mse_loss`, `criterion_neg_log_bernoulli` | Masked reconstruction and zero-inflation losses |
| **Training** | `scgpt.trainer` | `train`, `evaluate`, `prepare_data` | Training loops, data prep, SCIB metric evaluation |
| **Cell Embedding** | `scgpt.tasks.cell_emb` | `embed_data`, `get_batch_cell_embeddings` | Batch inference for cell-level embeddings |
| **GRN Inference** | `scgpt.tasks.grn` | `GeneEmbedding` | Gene similarity, metagene discovery from gene embeddings |
| **Data Bank** | `scgpt.scbank` | `DataBank`, `DataTable` | Large-scale dataset storage and flexible access |

Sources: [scgpt/__init__.py](scgpt/__init__.py#L18-L30), [scgpt/data_collator.py](scgpt/data_collator.py#L7-L50), [scgpt/loss.py](scgpt/loss.py#L1-L37), [scgpt/tasks/__init__.py](scgpt/tasks/__init__.py#L1-L3)

## How a Cell Becomes a Sequence

Understanding the tokenization pipeline is critical because it bridges the biological data format (AnnData) and the model's expected input (padded, binned token sequences). The `Preprocessor` transforms raw counts through a configurable pipeline — filtering low-count genes/cells, normalizing to a fixed total, applying log1p, selecting highly variable genes, and finally **binning** non-zero expression values into discrete bins using quantile-based binning. The `GeneVocab` then maps each gene name to a unique integer token. The `DataCollator` assembles per-cell sequences at training time: it prepends a `<cls>` token, pads to `max_length`, applies random masking (MLM), and bins values on-the-fly.

> [!TIP]
> The first bin in the binning scheme is always reserved for zero expression. Non-zero values are binned using quantile boundaries, so each gene's expression distribution is adaptively discretized. This design preserves the sparsity structure of scRNA-seq data.

Sources: [scgpt/preprocess.py](scgpt/preprocess.py#L139-L200), [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py](scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py#L21-L85), [scgpt/data_collator.py](scgpt/data_collator.py#L100-L170)

## Model Design Decisions

The `TransformerModel` exposes several configuration knobs that control how expression data is encoded and decoded. The most important are compared below.

| Parameter | Options | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `input_emb_style` | `continuous`, `category`, `scaling` | `continuous` | How gene and value embeddings combine. `continuous` = addition; `scaling` = element-wise multiplication; `category` = learned bin embeddings |
| `cell_emb_style` | `cls`, `avg-pool`, `w-pool` | `cls` | How to extract a cell-level vector from transformer output. `cls` uses the `<cls>` token position; `w-pool` uses expression-weighted average |
| `do_mvc` | `True` / `False` | `False` | Enable Masked Value Prediction for Cell embedding (MVC) decoder — reconstructs masked gene expressions from the cell embedding alone |
| `do_dab` | `True` / `False` | `False` | Enable Domain Adversarial Batch correction — a gradient-reversal discriminator that encourages batch-invariant embeddings |
| `explicit_zero_prob` | `True` / `False` | `False` | Model explicit zero-inflation by predicting a Bernoulli probability for each gene being zero |
| `use_fast_transformer` | `True` / `False` | `False` | Use Flash-Attention backend for faster and memory-efficient attention |
| `domain_spec_batchnorm` | `True`, `"dsbn"`, `"batchnorm"`, `False` | `False` | Apply domain-specific batch normalization per batch label |

> [!TIP]
> The `continuous` + `cls` combination is the default and most battle-tested configuration. Switch to `scaling` if you want the model to treat expression values as multiplicative scaling factors on gene embeddings — this can improve perturbation prediction tasks where expression fold-changes matter.

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py](scgpt/model/model.py#L25-L95), [scgpt/model/model.py](scgpt/model/model.py#L180-L260)

## Pretraining Objectives

scGPT is pretrained with a combination of self-supervised objectives that teach the model different facets of single-cell biology. During a forward pass, multiple objectives can be active simultaneously via boolean flags (`CLS`, `CCE`, `MVC`, `ECS`).

| Objective | Flag | What It Teaches | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Masked Gene Expression (MLM)** | always active | Reconstruct masked expression values | Randomly mask ~15% of gene tokens; decode via `ExprDecoder` |
| **Cell Type Classification (CLS)** | `CLS=True` | Discriminative cell-type awareness | `ClsDecoder` maps cell embedding → cell type logits |
| **Contrastive Cell Embedding (CCE)** | `CCE=True` | Robust cell-level representations | Two forward passes with dropout; cosine similarity contrastive loss |
| **Masked Value for Cell (MVC)** | `MVC=True` | Cell embedding sufficiency | `MVCDecoder` reconstructs masked gene expressions from cell embedding alone using inner-product or concat-query architecture |
| **Elastic Cell Similarity (ECS)** | `ECS=True` | Within-cell gene coherence | Penalizes low similarity among embeddings of genes from the same cell |

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py](scgpt/model/model.py#L290-L400), [scgpt/loss.py](scgpt/loss.py#L1-L37)

## Project Structure

The repository is organized so that the `scgpt/` package is the installable core, `tutorials/` provides end-to-end notebook walkthroughs, and `data/` contains scripts for building large-scale pretraining corpora.

```
scGPT/
├── scgpt/                          # 📦 Installable Python package
│   ├── model/
│   │   ├── model.py                # TransformerModel, encoders, decoders
│   │   ├── multiomic_model.py      # Multi-omic extension
│   │   ├── generation_model.py     # Perturbation generation model
│   │   ├── dsbn.py                 # Domain-specific batch normalization
│   │   ├── grad_reverse.py         # Gradient reversal for adversarial training
│   │   └── flash_attn_compat.py    # Flash-Attention compatibility layer
│   ├── tokenizer/
│   │   ├── gene_tokenizer.py       # GeneVocab class
│   │   ├── vocab_compat.py         # Cross-version Vocab compatibility
│   │   └── default_*.json          # Built-in vocabulary files
│   ├── tasks/
│   │   ├── cell_emb.py             # Cell embedding extraction
│   │   └── grn.py                  # Gene regulatory network inference
│   ├── scbank/                     # Large-scale data management
│   ├── preprocess.py               # Preprocessor pipeline
│   ├── data_collator.py            # Batch collation + MLM masking
│   ├── data_sampler.py             # SubsetsBatchSampler
│   ├── loss.py                     # Loss functions
│   ├── trainer.py                  # Training & evaluation loops
│   └── utils/                      # Utilities, pretrained model loading
│
├── tutorials/                      # 📓 Hands-on notebooks
│   ├── Tutorial_Annotation.ipynb
│   ├── Tutorial_Integration.ipynb
│   ├── Tutorial_Perturbation.ipynb
│   ├── Tutorial_GRN.ipynb
│   ├── Tutorial_Multiomics.ipynb
│   ├── Tutorial_Reference_Mapping.ipynb
│   └── zero-shot/                 # Zero-shot application notebooks
│
├── examples/                       # 🔧 Script-based fine-tuning example
│   └── finetune_integration.py
├── tests/                          # ✅ Unit tests
├── data/                           # 📊 Pretraining data build scripts
└── docs/                           # 📖 Sphinx documentation source
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/__init__.py](scgpt/model/__init__.py#L1-L12), [scgpt/tokenizer/__init__.py](scgpt/tokenizer/__init__.py#L1-L2), [scgpt/scbank/__init__.py](scgpt/scbank/__init__.py#L1-L20)

## Supported Downstream Tasks

scGPT's pretrained representations are designed to transfer across a wide range of single-cell analyses. The table summarizes each task, its tutorial entry point, and the model components involved.

| Task | Tutorial | Key Model Component | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cell Type Annotation** | `Tutorial_Annotation.ipynb` | `ClsDecoder` | Classify cell types in new datasets using fine-tuned classifier head |
| **Multi-Batch Integration** | `Tutorial_Integration.ipynb` | `ExprDecoder` + DAB | Remove batch effects while preserving biological variation |
| **Perturbation Prediction** | `Tutorial_Perturbation.ipynb` | `TransformerGenerator` | Predict post-perturbation expression from control cells |
| **Gene Regulatory Network** | `Tutorial_GRN.ipynb` / `Tutorial_Attention_GRN.ipynb` | `GeneEmbedding` / Attention weights | Infer gene–gene interactions from embeddings or attention maps |
| **Reference Mapping** | `Tutorial_Reference_Mapping.ipynb` | `embed_data` + FAISS | Map new cells to a reference atlas using cell embedding similarity |
| **Multi-omics Integration** | `Tutorial_Multiomics.ipynb` | `MultiOmicTransformerModel` | Jointly encode RNA + ATAC or other modality pairs |
| **Zero-Shot Applications** | `tutorials/zero-shot/` | `embed_data` | Use continually pretrained checkpoints without any fine-tuning |

Sources: [scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py](scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py#L20-L80), [scgpt/tasks/grn.py](scgpt/tasks/grn.py#L14-L60), [scgpt/model/generation_model.py](scgpt/model/generation_model.py#L30-L80), [README.md](README.md#L40-L60)

## Pretrained Model Zoo

scGPT ships with several pretrained checkpoints. The **whole-human** model, trained on 33 million normal human cells, is the recommended default for most applications. Organ-specific models (brain, blood, heart, lung, kidney) can outperform the general model when your fine-tuning data shares a similar tissue context. A separately **continual pretrained** checkpoint is optimized for zero-shot cell embedding tasks.

| Model | Training Data | Best For |
|---|---|---|
| `whole-human` (recommended) | 33M normal human cells | General-purpose fine-tuning |
| `continual pretrained` | Further pretraining for embeddings | Zero-shot cell embedding |
| `brain` | 13.2M brain cells | Neuroscience applications |
| `blood` | 10.3M blood & bone marrow cells | Hematology |
| `heart` | 1.8M heart cells | Cardiology |
| `lung` | 2.1M lung cells | Pulmonary research |
| `kidney` | 814K kidney cells | Nephrology |
| `pan-cancer` | 5.7M cancer cells | Oncology |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L57-L72)

# Quick Start



Get scGPT running in minutes. This page walks you through installation, a minimal working example, and the essential API surface you need to start fine-tuning a single-cell foundation model on your own data. By the end, you will have loaded a pretrained model, preprocessed an AnnData object, tokenized gene expression, and extracted cell embeddings — the core loop that underpins every scGPT workflow.

## How scGPT Works: The Big Picture

scGPT models each cell as a **sequence of gene–value token pairs** and processes them through a Transformer encoder. The architecture mirrors NLP's "token + embedding" paradigm, but here genes are tokens and binned expression values are their features. Understanding this data flow is the single most important mental model for working with scGPT.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Raw AnnData<br/>(cells × genes)"] --> B["Preprocessor<br/>normalize → log1p → HVG → bin"]
    B --> C["Tokenizer<br/>gene_ids + binned_values"]
    C --> D["TransformerModel<br/>GeneEncoder + ValueEncoder<br/>→ Transformer → Decoder"]
    D --> E["Outputs<br/>cell embeddings /<br/>class predictions /<br/>gene predictions"]
    style A fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3
    style B fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
    style C fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
    style D fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9C27B0
    style E fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#E91E63
```

The **Preprocessor** transforms raw counts into binned discrete values. The **Tokenizer** maps gene names to vocabulary indices and pairs them with those binned values. The **TransformerModel** encodes this sequence and can output cell embeddings, cell-type classifications, or reconstructed gene expressions depending on which decoder heads are enabled. Every downstream task — integration, annotation, perturbation prediction, GRN inference — is a variation on this same pipeline.

Sources: [scgpt/preprocess.py](/scgpt/preprocess.py#L24-L100), [scgpt/model/model.py](/scgpt/model/model.py#L21-L153), [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py](/scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py#L293-L400)

## Installation

scGPT requires **Python ≥ 3.7.12** and **PyTorch ≥ 1.13**. Install the core package from PyPI:

```bash
pip install scgpt
```

For GPU-accelerated attention (strongly recommended for training), add the optional flash-attn dependency:

```bash
pip install scgpt "flash-attn<1.0.5"
```

> [!TIP]
> If `flash-attn` fails to install, it is usually a CUDA version mismatch. scGPT will gracefully fall back to PyTorch's native attention — you can set `use_fast_transformer=False` when constructing the model. See the [flash-attn repo](https://github.com/HazyResearch/flash-attention) for compatible CUDA versions.

Optionally, install [wandb](https://wandb.ai/) for experiment tracking:

```bash
pip install wandb
```

| Dependency | Minimum Version | Purpose |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `torch` | ≥ 1.13.0 | Core deep learning framework |
| `scanpy` | ≥ 1.9.1 | Single-cell data I/O and preprocessing |
| `scvi-tools` | ≥ 0.16.0 | Benchmark datasets and evaluation |
| `pandas` | ≥ 1.3.5 | Data manipulation |
| `datasets` | ≥ 2.20.0 | HuggingFace data loading |
| `flash-attn` | ≥ 2.8.0 (optional) | Fast GPU attention kernel |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L62), [README.md](/README.md#L28-L45)

## Step-by-Step: Your First scGPT Pipeline

The following minimal example demonstrates the complete workflow from raw data to cell embeddings. Each step maps directly to the architecture diagram above.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1["1. Load Data"] --> S2["2. Build Vocabulary"]
    S2 --> S3["3. Preprocess & Bin"]
    S3 --> S4["4. Tokenize"]
    S4 --> S5["5. Load Pretrained Model"]
    S5 --> S6["6. Get Cell Embeddings"]
    style S1 fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565C0
    style S2 fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565C0
    style S3 fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2E7D32
    style S4 fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2E7D32
    style S5 fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#E65100
    style S6 fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#E65100
```

### Step 1 — Load Your Data

scGPT consumes [AnnData](https://anndata.readthedocs.io/) objects, the standard container in the single-cell ecosystem. Gene names must be stored in `adata.var` with a known column name.

```python
import scanpy as sc

adata = sc.read("your_data.h5ad")  # or any scanpy loader
adata.var["gene_name"] = adata.var.index.tolist()  # ensure gene names column exists
```

### Step 2 — Build or Load the Gene Vocabulary

The **GeneVocab** maps each gene symbol to a unique integer ID. When loading a pretrained model, you **must** use the vocabulary that was saved alongside the checkpoint to ensure gene–ID alignment.

```python
from scgpt.tokenizer.gene_tokenizer import GeneVocab
from pathlib import Path

# Load the vocabulary from a pretrained checkpoint folder
vocab = GeneVocab.from_file(Path("save/scGPT_human/vocab.json"))

# Add special tokens required for processing
special_tokens = ["<pad>", "<cls>", "<eoc>"]
for s in special_tokens:
    if s not in vocab:
        vocab.append_token(s)
vocab.set_default_index(vocab["<pad>"])
```

Cross-check your data against the vocabulary to retain only genes the model knows:

```python
import numpy as np

adata.var["id_in_vocab"] = [
    1 if gene in vocab else -1 for gene in adata.var["gene_name"]
]
adata = adata[:, adata.var["id_in_vocab"] >= 0]
print(f"Matched {np.sum(adata.var['id_in_vocab'] >= 0)} genes in vocabulary")
```

Sources: [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py](/scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py#L113-L160), [tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb](/tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb)

### Step 3 — Preprocess and Bin Expression Values

The **Preprocessor** orchestrates a configurable pipeline: filtering → normalization → log1p → HVG selection → binning. Binning converts continuous expression into discrete bins (the first bin is reserved for zeros), which is the format scGPT expects as input.

```python
from scgpt.preprocess import Preprocessor

preprocessor = Preprocessor(
    use_key="X",                    # use raw counts from adata.X
    filter_gene_by_counts=3,        # remove low-count genes
    normalize_total=1e4,            # depth normalization to 10,000
    log1p=True,                     # log1p transform
    subset_hvg=1200,                # keep top 1200 highly variable genes
    hvg_flavor="seurat_v3",        # HVG selection method
    binning=51,                     # bin into 51 discrete values
)
preprocessor(adata, batch_key="str_batch")
```

The preprocessor stores results in `adata.layers` — binned values go to `adata.layers["X_binned"]` by default.

| Preprocessor Parameter | Default | Purpose |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `filter_gene_by_counts` | `False` | Minimum total counts to keep a gene |
| `filter_cell_by_counts` | `False` | Minimum total counts to keep a cell |
| `normalize_total` | `1e4` | Target sum for depth normalization |
| `log1p` | `False` | Apply log(1+x) transform |
| `subset_hvg` | `False` | Number of HVGs to retain |
| `binning` | `None` | Number of discrete bins for quantile binning |

Sources: [scgpt/preprocess.py](/scgpt/preprocess.py#L24-L100), [scgpt/preprocess.py](/scgpt/preprocess.py#L101-L230)

### Step 4 — Tokenize the Data

Tokenization pairs each gene's vocabulary ID with its binned expression value, producing the `(gene_ids, values)` tensor pairs that the Transformer consumes.

```python
from scgpt.tokenizer import tokenize_and_pad_batch, random_mask_value
from scipy.sparse import issparse

pad_token = "<pad>"
pad_value = -2
mask_value = -1
max_seq_len = 1201  # n_hvg + 1 (for <cls> token)

input_layer_key = "X_binned"
all_counts = (
    adata.layers[input_layer_key].toarray()
    if issparse(adata.layers[input_layer_key])
    else adata.layers[input_layer_key]
)
genes = adata.var["gene_name"].tolist()
gene_ids = np.array(vocab(genes), dtype=int)

tokenized = tokenize_and_pad_batch(
    all_counts,
    gene_ids,
    max_len=max_seq_len,
    vocab=vocab,
    pad_token=pad_token,
    pad_value=pad_value,
    append_cls=True,          # prepend <cls> token
    include_zero_gene=True,   # include zero-expression genes
)
# tokenized["genes"]  → Tensor of gene IDs, shape (n_cells, max_seq_len)
# tokenized["values"] → Tensor of binned values, shape (n_cells, max_seq_len)
```

For training, apply random masking to create the masked-language-model objective:

```python
masked_values = random_mask_value(
    tokenized["values"],
    mask_ratio=0.4,
    mask_value=mask_value,
    pad_value=pad_value,
)
```

Sources: [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py](/scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py#L293-L400), [tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb](/tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb)

### Step 5 — Load a Pretrained Model

The **TransformerModel** is the central scGPT architecture. When fine-tuning, load the pretrained weights and model config from a checkpoint directory containing `best_model.pt` and `args.json`.

```python
import json
import torch
from scgpt.model import TransformerModel
from scgpt.utils import load_pretrained

model_dir = Path("save/scGPT_human")

# Read model architecture from the checkpoint's saved config
with open(model_dir / "args.json", "r") as f:
    model_configs = json.load(f)

model = TransformerModel(
    ntoken=len(vocab),
    d_model=model_configs["embsize"],
    nhead=model_configs["nheads"],
    d_hid=model_configs["d_hid"],
    nlayers=model_configs["nlayers"],
    nlayers_cls=model_configs["n_layers_cls"],
    n_cls=1,                             # adjust for your number of cell types
    vocab=vocab,
    dropout=0.2,
    pad_token="<pad>",
    pad_value=-2,
    do_mvc=False,
    do_dab=True,                         # enable domain adversarial for batch correction
    use_batch_labels=True,
    num_batch_labels=num_batch_types,
    input_emb_style="continuous",
    n_input_bins=51,
    cell_emb_style="cls",
    use_fast_transformer=True,
)

# Load pretrained weights (non-strict: skips mismatched or new heads)
load_pretrained(model, torch.load(model_dir / "best_model.pt"), strict=False)
model.eval()
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py](/scgpt/model/model.py#L21-L153), [scgpt/utils/util.py](/scgpt/utils/util.py#L238-L310)

### Step 6 — Extract Cell Embeddings

With the model loaded and data tokenized, extracting cell embeddings is a single forward pass. The `<cls>` token's output representation serves as the cell-level embedding by default.

```python
with torch.no_grad():
    output = model(
        src=tokenized["genes"],
        values=tokenized["values"],
        src_key_padding_mask=tokenized["genes"] == vocab["<pad>"],
    )
    cell_embeddings = output["cell_emb"]  # shape: (n_cells, d_model)
```

These embeddings can then be used for UMAP visualization, clustering, cell-type classification, or any downstream analysis.

> [!TIP]
> The `cell_emb_style` parameter controls how cell embeddings are extracted from the Transformer output: `"cls"` uses the `<cls>` token position, `"avg-pool"` averages across all gene positions, and `"w-pool"` applies a weighted sum. The pretrained models use `"cls"` — stick with it unless you have a specific reason to change.

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py](/scgpt/model/model.py#L192-L210), [scgpt/model/model.py](/scgpt/model/model.py#L294-L350)

## Essential API Reference

Below is a quick-reference table of the most frequently used scGPT classes and functions, organized by pipeline stage.

| Stage | Import | Description |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Preprocessing** | `scgpt.preprocess.Preprocessor` | Configurable pipeline: filter → normalize → log1p → HVG → bin |
| **Vocabulary** | `scgpt.tokenizer.gene_tokenizer.GeneVocab` | Gene symbol ↔ integer ID mapping |
| **Tokenization** | `scgpt.tokenizer.tokenize_and_pad_batch` | Convert binned expression to (gene_ids, values) tensors |
| **Masking** | `scgpt.tokenizer.random_mask_value` | Randomly mask values for MLM training objective |
| **Model** | `scgpt.model.TransformerModel` | Core Transformer with gene/value encoders and task decoders |
| **Loading** | `scgpt.utils.load_pretrained` | Load checkpoint weights with flash-attn / PyTorch backend compatibility |
| **Training** | `scgpt.trainer.train` | Training loop with wandb logging |
| **Seeding** | `scgpt.utils.set_seed` | Set reproducible random seeds across numpy and torch |

Sources: [scgpt/__init__.py](/scgpt/__init__.py#L1-L30), [scgpt/model/__init__.py](/scgpt/model/__init__.py#L1-L12), [scgpt/tokenizer/__init__.py](/scgpt/tokenizer/__init__.py#L1-L2)

# Pretrained Model Zoo



scGPT provides a collection of pretrained checkpoints that serve as starting points for a wide range of single-cell analysis tasks. Each checkpoint encodes knowledge learned from millions of cells during self-supervised pretraining, and can be either used directly for **zero-shot** inference or further **fine-tuned** on your downstream dataset. This page catalogues every available checkpoint, explains what each one contains, and walks you through the mechanics of loading and selecting the right model for your work.

## Available Checkpoints

The table below lists all officially released scGPT checkpoints. The **whole-human** model is the general-purpose default—start there unless your downstream data aligns closely with one of the organ-specific or specialised distributions.

| Model | Training Data | Description | Recommended Use | Download |
|:------|:-------------|:------------|:----------------|:---------|
| **whole-human** ★ | 33M normal human cells | Pretrained on the largest and most diverse normal human cell corpus | Default for all tasks; fine-tuning & zero-shot | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1oWh_-ZRdhtoGQ2Fw24HP41FgLoomVo-y) |
| **continual pretrained** | whole-human + Tabula Sapiens labels | Further supervised with cell-type labels during a continual pretraining stage | Zero-shot cell embedding, integration, reference mapping | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1_GROJTzXiAV8HB4imruOTk6PEGuNOcgB) |
| **brain** | 13.2M brain cells | Organ-specific pretraining | Brain-focused datasets | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1vf1ijfQSk7rGdDGpBntR5bi5g6gNt-Gx) |
| **blood** | 10.3M blood & bone marrow cells | Organ-specific pretraining | Hematopoietic / immune datasets | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1kkug5C7NjvXIwQGGaGoqXTk_Lb_pDrBU) |
| **heart** | 1.8M heart cells | Organ-specific pretraining | Cardiac datasets | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1GcgXrd7apn6y4Ze_iSCncskX3UsWPY2r) |
| **lung** | 2.1M lung cells | Organ-specific pretraining | Pulmonary datasets | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/16A1DJ30PT6bodt4bWLa4hpS7gbWZQFBG) |
| **kidney** | 814K kidney cells | Organ-specific pretraining | Renal datasets | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1S-1AR65DF120kNFpEbWCvRHPhpkGK3kK) |
| **pan-cancer** | 5.7M cancer cells (various types) | Pretrained on diverse cancer cell populations | Tumour / cancer-focused datasets | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/13QzLHilYUd0v3HTwa_9n4G4yEF-hdkqa) |

> [!TIP]
> When your fine-tuning dataset shares similar cell-type context with an organ-specific model's training data, that organ-specific checkpoint often converges faster and achieves better performance than the general whole-human model.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L56-L72), [tutorials/zero-shot/README.md](/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md#L1-L29)

## Checkpoint Structure

Every downloaded checkpoint folder contains three files that scGPT expects in a fixed layout. Understanding this structure is essential for both loading models correctly and debugging loading failures.

```
scGPT_human/              ← checkpoint folder (name may vary)
├── args.json             ← model architecture hyperparameters
├── best_model.pt         ← model state_dict (PyTorch checkpoint)
└── vocab.json            ← gene token → index mapping (≈60K genes)
```

| File | Format | Purpose |
|:-----|:-------|:--------|
| `args.json` | JSON dict | Stores architecture dimensions (`embsize`, `nheads`, `d_hid`, `nlayers`, `n_layers_cls`) that override any manually-specified model config during loading |
| `best_model.pt` | PyTorch `state_dict` | All learned weights—gene embeddings, transformer layers, decoders |
| `vocab.json` | JSON `{token: index}` | Maps gene symbol strings to integer token IDs; the whole-human vocabulary contains ~60,697 entries |

Sources: [tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb](/tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb#L322-L350), [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py](/scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py#L106-L127)

## How to Choose a Model

The decision flow below helps you pick the right checkpoint for your scenario. The key differentiator is whether you need **zero-shot** embeddings (no training at all) or are willing to **fine-tune** on your target dataset.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start: Choose a Checkpoint] --> B{Do you need zero-shot inference?}
    B -- Yes --> C{Is cell embedding the primary goal?}
    C -- Yes --> D[Use continual pretrained model]
    C -- No --> E[Use whole-human model]
    B -- No --> F{Does your data match an organ-specific domain?}
    F -- Yes --> G[Use the organ-specific checkpoint]
    F -- No --> H[Use whole-human model]
    D --> I[Download & load checkpoint]
    E --> I
    G --> I
    H --> I
    I --> J{Zero-shot or fine-tune?}
    J -- Zero-shot --> K[Call embed_data directly]
    J -- Fine-tune --> L[Load with load_pretrained, then train]
```

### Zero-shot vs. Fine-tuning at a Glance

| Aspect | Zero-shot | Fine-tuning |
|:-------|:----------|:------------|
| Training required | None | 10–30 epochs on your data |
| Speed | Seconds to minutes | Minutes to hours (GPU) |
| When to prefer | Quick exploration; limited compute; large pretraining overlap | Small domain shift; best accuracy needed; novel cell types |
| Recommended model | Continual pretrained (embedding tasks) or whole-human | Organ-specific if available, else whole-human |
| Output | Cell embeddings stored in `adata.obsm["X_scGPT"]` | Full model with task-specific decoders |

Sources: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb](/tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb#L1-L36), [tutorials/zero-shot/README.md](/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md#L11-L18)

## Loading a Pretrained Model

### Step 1 — Download and Extract

Download your chosen checkpoint folder from the Google Drive link in the table above, and place it in a local directory (e.g., `save/scGPT_human/`).

### Step 2 — Load Vocabulary and Architecture Config

The vocabulary and model dimensions are loaded from the checkpoint's own files, ensuring exact compatibility:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from scgpt.tokenizer.gene_tokenizer import GeneVocab
import json

model_dir = Path("save/scGPT_human")
vocab_file = model_dir / "vocab.json"
model_config_file = model_dir / "args.json"
model_file = model_dir / "best_model.pt"

# Load vocabulary
vocab = GeneVocab.from_file(vocab_file)
# Ensure special tokens are present
special_tokens = ["<pad>", "<cls>", "<eoc>"]
for s in special_tokens:
    if s not in vocab:
        vocab.append_token(s)

# Load architecture config (overrides manual hyperparameters)
with open(model_config_file, "r") as f:
    model_configs = json.load(f)
```

Sources: [tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb](/tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb#L322-L357), [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py](/scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py#L106-L127)

### Step 3 — Instantiate the Model and Load Weights

Create a `TransformerModel` with the architecture parameters from `args.json`, then call `load_pretrained` to inject the saved weights. The `load_pretrained` utility automatically handles **parameter renaming** between flash-attention and standard PyTorch backends, so you can load the same checkpoint on CPU, GPU, or flash-attention hardware:

```python
import torch
from scgpt.model import TransformerModel
from scgpt.utils import load_pretrained

ntokens = len(vocab)
model = TransformerModel(
    ntokens,
    model_configs["embsize"],       # embedding dimension
    model_configs["nheads"],        # number of attention heads
    model_configs["d_hid"],         # feed-forward hidden dimension
    model_configs["nlayers"],       # number of transformer layers
    vocab=vocab,
    dropout=0.2,
    pad_token="<pad>",
    pad_value=0,
    do_mvc=True,                    # enable MVC decoder for integration
    do_dab=True,                    # enable adversarial batch correction
    use_batch_labels=True,
    num_batch_labels=num_batch_types,  # from your dataset
    domain_spec_batchnorm=True,
    n_input_bins=51,
    ecs_threshold=0.8,
    explicit_zero_prob=True,
    use_fast_transformer=True,      # flash-attn if available
    pre_norm=False,
)

# Load pretrained weights (handles flash-attn ↔ PyTorch key remapping)
load_pretrained(model, torch.load(model_file), verbose=False)
model.to(device)
```

Sources: [scgpt/utils/util.py](/scgpt/utils/util.py#L290-L360), [scgpt/model/model.py](/scgpt/model/model.py#L12-L99), [tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb](/tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb#L672-L697)

### How `load_pretrained` Works Internally

The `load_pretrained` function performs three critical operations automatically:

1. **Backend-aware key renaming** — When flash-attention is not used, attention weight keys like `self_attn.Wqkv.` are renamed to `self_attn.in_proj_` (the standard PyTorch naming). When flash-attention *is* used, the reverse or version-specific renaming rules are applied. This means the same `best_model.pt` file works on any backend.

2. **Prefix filtering** (optional) — If you pass a `prefix` list, only parameters whose keys start with one of those prefixes are loaded. This is useful for partial transfer (e.g., loading only the encoder).

3. **Shape-safe partial loading** — In non-strict mode (the default), parameters whose shapes do not match the current model are silently skipped. This prevents crashes when the downstream task uses a different number of class labels or batch labels than the pretrained model.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[best_model.pt] --> B{Detect backend}
    B -- Flash-attn --> C[Apply flash-attn rename rules]
    B -- PyTorch std --> D[Apply PyTorch rename rules]
    C --> E[Filter by prefix?]
    D --> E
    E -- Yes --> F[Keep matching keys only]
    E -- No --> G[Keep all keys]
    F --> H{Strict mode?}
    G --> H
    H -- Yes --> I[Exact match load]
    H -- No --> J[Shape-safe partial load]
    I --> K[Model ready]
    J --> K
```

Sources: [scgpt/utils/util.py](/scgpt/utils/util.py#L290-L360), [scgpt/model/flash_attn_compat.py](/scgpt/model/flash_attn_compat.py)

## Zero-shot Embedding

For zero-shot applications, you can skip manual model construction and use the high-level `embed_data` function, which handles preprocessing, tokenization, and batched encoding in a single call:

```python
import scgpt as scg

# Zero-shot embedding — no training required
embed_adata = scg.tasks.embed_data(
    adata,
    model_dir,
    gene_col="gene_name",
    batch_key="sample",
)
# Embeddings are stored in embed_adata.obsm["X_scGPT"]
```

The continual pretrained checkpoint is specifically optimised for zero-shot cell embedding tasks—it inherits the whole-human weights and was further supervised with cell-type labels from Tabula Sapiens, which improves the biological structure of the embedding space.

> [!TIP]
> Zero-shot inference is extremely fast (seconds to minutes) and is a great first step. If the zero-shot results already meet your needs, fine-tuning may be unnecessary.

Sources: [scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py](/scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py), [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb](/tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb#L100-L200), [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration_Continual_Pretraining.ipynb](/tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration_Continual_Pretraining.ipynb#L1-L45)

## Vocabulary and Gene Compatibility

Each checkpoint ships with its own `vocab.json` that maps gene symbols to integer token IDs. The whole-human vocabulary covers **60,697 genes**, while organ-specific models may use slightly smaller vocabularies tailored to their tissue. When loading a pretrained model, you **must** use the vocabulary from the same checkpoint folder—mismatched vocabularies will produce incorrect token mappings.

### Cross-checking Genes with Your Dataset

After loading the vocabulary, you should verify how many of your dataset's genes are covered. Genes not found in the vocabulary will be filtered out before fine-tuning:

```python
adata.var["id_in_vocab"] = [
    1 if gene in vocab else -1 for gene in adata.var["gene_name"]
]
gene_ids_in_vocab = np.array(adata.var["id_in_vocab"])
print(f"Match {np.sum(gene_ids_in_vocab >= 0)}/{len(gene_ids_in_vocab)} genes "
      f"in vocabulary of size {len(vocab)}.")
# Keep only genes that exist in the vocabulary
adata = adata[:, adata.var["id_in_vocab"] >= 0]
```

A typical PBMC 10K dataset retains approximately 97% of its genes (~3,256 out of 3,346) against the whole-human vocabulary. If your retention rate is significantly lower, verify that your gene naming convention (e.g., Ensembl IDs vs. gene symbols) matches the vocabulary format.

Sources: [tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb](/tutorials/Tutorial_Integration.ipynb#L322-L340), [scgpt/tokenizer/default_gene_vocab.json](/scgpt/tokenizer/default_gene_vocab.json#L1-L30)

## Model Architecture at a Glance

All checkpoints share the same `TransformerModel` architecture—the differences lie only in the training data and the learned weights. The architecture is configured by the parameters stored in each checkpoint's `args.json`:

| Parameter | Description | Typical Value (whole-human) |
|:----------|:------------|:---------------------------|
| `embsize` | Gene & value embedding dimension | 128–512 |
| `nheads` | Number of multi-head attention heads | 4–8 |
| `d_hid` | Feed-forward hidden dimension | 128–512 |
| `nlayers` | Number of transformer encoder layers | 4–12 |
| `n_layers_cls` | Number of layers in the classification decoder | 3 |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input
        GE[GeneEncoder] --> TE[Token Embedding]
        VE[ValueEncoder] --> VE2[Value Embedding]
    end
    TE --> SUM["⊕ Combine"]
    SUM --> DSBN["Domain-Specific BatchNorm"]
    DSBN --> TX["Transformer Encoder × nlayers"]
    TX --> EXPR["ExprDecoder — gene expression reconstruction"]
    TX --> CLS["ClsDecoder — cell type classification"]
    TX --> MVC["MVCDecoder — masked value prediction for cell emb"]
    TX --> DAB["AdversarialDiscriminator — batch correction"]
    TX --> CCE["Contrastive Cell Embedding"]
    TX --> ECS["Elastic Cell Similarity"]
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py](/scgpt/model/model.py#L12-L99), [scgpt/model/__init__.py](/scgpt/model/__init__.py#L1-L12)

## Known Limitations

The pretrained models are trained with purely self-supervised objectives (gene expression reconstruction), which means they may **not fully mitigate type II technical batch effects**—distribution shifts driven by sequencing procedures rather than biology. If your downstream task is highly sensitive to batch correction, consider enabling the DAB (Domain Adversarial Batch correction) and DSBN (Domain-Specific Batch Normalisation) objectives during fine-tuning, or evaluate whether the continual pretrained model's supervised cell-type knowledge offers better zero-shot separation.

Sources: [tutorials/zero-shot/README.md](/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md#L22-L29)

## Next Steps

Now that you understand the model zoo and how to load checkpoints, you are ready to apply scGPT to your own data:

- **[Quick Start](2-quick-start)** — End-to-end walkthrough from installation to your first embedding
